John Brown. A radical abolitionist whose violent tactics and ultimate execution transformed him into a martyr for the antislavery cause. His 1859 raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, intended to spark a slave rebellion, failed militarily but succeeded in galvanizing the nation toward civil war. Hailed as a hero by abolitionists and condemned as a terrorist by the South, Brown embodied the polarization that made peaceful compromise impossible.

Born in Connecticut in 1800, he became deeply religious and devoted himself entirely to the abolition of slavery. He believed that slavery could only be destroyed through violence and was willing to shed blood—both slaveholders' and his own—to achieve emancipation. During the Kansas-Nebraska violence of the eighteen-fifties, he participated in pro-abolition militias, earning the nickname Old Brown. In October 1859, he led an armed band of followers, including his own sons, in a raid on the Harpers Ferry armory seeking to arm enslaved people. After a three-day siege, he was captured, tried for treason against Virginia, and executed by hanging in December 1859. His execution made him a symbol of Northern commitment to antislavery and a rallying cry for Southern secession. More broadly, his actions and the violent resistance they provoked represented the radical wing of abolitionism, ultimately justifying the movement's most extreme claims about the irreconcilability of slavery and the American republic.
